questions.ask: Write the action plan for bed 3 from its latest scan.

runs.text:
Bed 3's tomatoes have confirmed early blight on the upper leaves and a few stems at the east end, and the fruit is still clean. The bed has already had the last copper spray the farm's procedure allows this season, so this plan uses only non-chemical steps: remove spotted leaves, keep the leaves dry with morning drip watering, refresh the mulch and pull nightshade weeds and volunteer tomatoes. Check the bed every few days. After harvest, clear all plant debris and rotate tomato-family crops out of bed 3, then choose resistant varieties and test the soil for next season.

Remove infected leaves at the east end

Cut off leaves and branches with target-ring spots, starting with the upper leaves and stems at the east end where the blight sits. Work when the plants are dry. Bag the cuttings and take them out of the garden; don't compost them or leave them on the bed. Clean your pruners between plants. Repeat whenever new spotted leaves appear.

Keep the leaves dry with morning drip watering

Water only through the drip line along the north edge, early in the morning, so the leaves are dry by midday. Don't water from above; splashing carries spores from leaf to leaf. The west end sits low and dries slowly after rain, so keep standing water away from it and avoid working among wet plants there.

Refresh the mulch under the plants

Top up the organic mulch (straw, chopped leaves or grass clippings) under the plants so bare soil is covered. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the lower leaves.

Pull nightshade weeds and volunteer tomatoes

Pull weeds in and around bed 3, especially black nightshade, and pull any self-sown tomato seedlings. They can carry early blight and keep it going into next season.

Check the bed for new spots

Walk the whole bed and look for new target-ring spots, spots moving west past the east end, dark lesions on stems, and any spots on the fruit. Bed 3 has already had its last copper spray allowed this season under the farm's SOP, so no more copper goes on this year; if the blight spreads fast, ask your local extension office for advice.

Clear the bed after harvest and plan the rotation

After the last harvest, pull out all the tomato plants and fallen leaves from bed 3 and take them out of the garden, since the disease survives on old plant bits in the soil. Don't plant tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplant in bed 3 for the next two seasons, and don't move next year's tomatoes into a bed that just had peppers. Corn or another grass-family crop is a good choice before tomatoes come back.

Choose early blight resistant varieties for next year

When ordering seed or transplants for next year, choose tomato varieties listed as resistant or tolerant to early blight, and buy certified disease-free seed and plants.

Test the soil before next season

Test the soil where next year's tomatoes will grow. Keep potassium at a good level and lime only as the soil test advises; well-fed plants get less severe early blight. Follow the soil test and the fertiliser label.

New target-ring spots spreading west past the east end within a week

Spots or dark sunken patches appearing on the fruit at any time

Dark lesions on stems that grow or circle the stem over the next week

Most of the upper leaves yellowing or dropping within two weeks despite pruning

Ring spots showing up on the lower leaves early next season, which would mean the disease carried over

runs.text:
Bed 3 has confirmed early blight. The latest field report says it is still at the east end and the fruit is clean. Bed 3 has already had its sixth copper spray this season, the farm's SOP limit, so this plan relies on non-chemical steps. Remove spotted leaves, keep the leaves dry with early-morning drip watering, top up the mulch, pull weeds and volunteer tomatoes, and check the bed every few days. After harvest, clear the debris and plan next year: rotate crops, test the soil and choose resistant varieties.

Cut off spotted leaves and stems and throw them away

Start at the east end, where the target-ring spots have been. Cut off leaves and stems with spots and bag them. Do not compost them. Do it when the plants are dry, and clean your pruners before moving on to healthy plants so you don't spread spores along the bed.

Keep the leaves dry: drip in the early morning only

Water only through the drip line along the north edge, in the early morning, so the leaves are dry by midday. Don't water from above. The west end sits low and stays wet after rain, so check it for standing water and lead the water away.

Top up the mulch under the plants

Cover any bare soil under the plants with organic mulch such as straw or chopped leaves. Mulch stops rain splashing spores from the soil up onto the lower leaves.

Pull weeds and volunteer tomatoes around the bed

Pull weeds in and around bed 3, especially black nightshade, and any self-sown tomatoes. These plants carry early blight from one season to the next.

Check the bed for new spots every 3 days

Walk the whole bed. Look for new target-ring spots, spots moving west from the east end, and dark sunken spots on stems or fruit. Note what you find in #field-reports. The spray log shows bed 3 has had its sixth copper spray, the season limit in the farm's SOP, so don't plan another copper spray this season. If spots reach the fruit or spread fast, ask your local extension office what to do next.

Clear the debris and plan a 3-year rotation for bed 3

When the crop is finished, clear out the old vines and leaves, because the disease survives in old plant debris. Next year, don't grow tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplant in bed 3. Wait three years before growing them there again. Corn or another grass-family crop is a good choice for this bed.

Test the soil and keep potassium at a good level

Test the soil before next season. Keep potassium at a good level, and add lime only if the test advises it. Follow the soil test advice and the fertiliser label.

Choose early blight-resistant varieties for next year

When you choose next year's tomatoes, pick varieties that are resistant or tolerant to early blight. Buy certified disease-free seed or transplants.

New target-ring spots west of the east end within the next two weeks.

Dark sunken spots on fruit or stems at any check.

Many leaves yellowing and dropping within a week despite removing the spotted ones.

New spots on leaves you had cleared, within a week of a wet spell.

Bed 3 has confirmed early blight at the east end, and the fruit is still clean. The bed has had its sixth copper spray of the season, the farm's limit, so this plan uses no more fungicide this year. Remove spotted leaves, keep the leaves dry with morning drip watering, mulch, pull weeds and check the bed every few days. At the end of the season, clear the bed and rotate tomatoes elsewhere next year. If you're unsure about new symptoms, take a clear photo or ask your local extension office.

Remove spotted leaves

Cut off leaves and branches with target-ring spots, starting at the east end where the blight has been. Work when the leaves are dry, bag the cuttings and take them out of the garden; don't compost them. Clean your pruners between plants.

Keep the leaves dry

Water only through the drip line along the north edge, in the early morning, so the leaves are dry by midday. Don't water from above; splashing spreads spores from leaf to leaf.

Mulch bare soil

Spread organic mulch such as straw or chopped leaves over bare soil under the plants. It stops spores in the soil splashing up onto the lower leaves.

Check for new spots

Walk the whole bed and look for new target-ring spots on leaves and stems, especially toward the west end, and check the fruit. Remove new spotted leaves as you find them. No more copper this season: the bed has had its sixth spray, the farm's limit.

Pull weeds and volunteers

Pull weeds in and around the bed, especially black nightshade, and pull up any volunteer tomatoes. They can carry early blight.

Drain the west end after heavy rain

The west end of the bed sits low and dries slowly. After heavy rain, clear standing water from it quickly so the plants aren't stressed and the leaves dry sooner.

Clear the bed and plan rotation

At the end of the season, remove all tomato plants and fallen leaves from the bed and take them out of the garden. Next year, don't plant tomatoes, peppers, potatoes or eggplant here; grow them in this spot only once every three years, with a crop such as corn in between.

Choose resistant varieties for next year

When ordering seed for next year, choose tomato varieties that are resistant or tolerant to early blight, and buy certified seed or plants.

Spots or dark sunken patches on the fruit at any point.

plan.summary: Bed 3 has confirmed early blight at the east end, and the fruit is still clean. The bed has had its sixth copper spray of the season, the farm's limit, so this plan uses no more fungicide this year. Remove spotted leaves, keep the leaves dry with morning drip watering, mulch, pull weeds and check the bed every few days. At the end of the season, clear the bed and rotate tomatoes elsewhere next year. If you're unsure about new symptoms, take a clear photo or ask your local extension office.

steps.title: Remove spotted leaves
steps.detail: Cut off leaves and branches with target-ring spots, starting at the east end where the blight has been. Work when the leaves are dry, bag the cuttings and take them out of the garden; don't compost them. Clean your pruners between plants.

steps.title: Keep the leaves dry
steps.detail: Water only through the drip line along the north edge, in the early morning, so the leaves are dry by midday. Don't water from above; splashing spreads spores from leaf to leaf.

steps.title: Mulch bare soil
steps.detail: Spread organic mulch such as straw or chopped leaves over bare soil under the plants. It stops spores in the soil splashing up onto the lower leaves.

steps.title: Check for new spots
steps.detail: Walk the whole bed and look for new target-ring spots on leaves and stems, especially toward the west end, and check the fruit. Remove new spotted leaves as you find them. No more copper this season: the bed has had its sixth spray, the farm's limit.

steps.title: Pull weeds and volunteers
steps.detail: Pull weeds in and around the bed, especially black nightshade, and pull up any volunteer tomatoes. They can carry early blight.

steps.title: Drain the west end after heavy rain
steps.detail: The west end of the bed sits low and dries slowly. After heavy rain, clear standing water from it quickly so the plants aren't stressed and the leaves dry sooner.

steps.title: Clear the bed and plan rotation
steps.detail: At the end of the season, remove all tomato plants and fallen leaves from the bed and take them out of the garden. Next year, don't plant tomatoes, peppers, potatoes or eggplant here; grow them in this spot only once every three years, with a crop such as corn in between.

steps.title: Choose resistant varieties for next year
steps.detail: When ordering seed for next year, choose tomato varieties that are resistant or tolerant to early blight, and buy certified seed or plants.

watch_for: New target-ring spots spreading past the east end toward the west end within a week of removing spotted leaves.
Spots or dark sunken patches on the fruit at any point.
Lower and middle leaves yellowing and dropping across the bed within two weeks.
